etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lepen, from Old English hlēapan, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną. Doublet of lope, lowp, elope, gallop, galop, interlope, and loop.

Cognate with West Frisian ljeppe (“to jump”), Dutch lopen (“to run; to walk”), German laufen (“to run; to walk”), Danish løbe (“to run”), Norwegian Bokmål løpe (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *klewb- (“to spring, stumble”) (compare Lithuanian šlùbti ‘to become lame’, klùbti ‘to stumble’).

quote.text: It is grete nede a man to go bak to recouer the better his leep

quote.citation: 1600, anonymous author, The wisdome of Doctor Dodypoll, act 4:
quote.text: I, I defie thee: wert not thou next him when he leapt into the Riuer?

quote.citation: 1783, Hugh Blair, from the “Iliad” in Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, lecture 4, page 65
quote.text: Th’ infernal monarch rear’d his horrid head, Leapt from his throne, lest Neptune’s arm should lay His dark dominions open to the day.

quote.citation: 1999, Ai, Vice: New & Selected Poems, page 78
quote.text: It is better to leap into the void.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pass over by a leap or jump.

definitions.definition: (archaic, transitive) To copulate with (a female beast)

definitions.definition: The distance traversed by a leap or jump.

quote.text: Manikanta returned to the palace riding on a royal tiger accompanied by a leap of leopards to the utter surprise of the inhabitants of Pantalam.

quote.citation: 2005 July 23, Next Windows to be named "Vista".‎[3]:
quote.text: I can see it now... a leap of Leopards eating the carcass of a Longhorn out in the Vista....

quote.citation: 2009, Cooper, The President's Dilemma: A Novel‎[4], page 131:
quote.text: Without the Chop Chop Chop Chop Cowville seems almost normal: no hover of helicopters, no leap of leopards.

quote.text: I felt like the only one of my kind, and all around me were the other kids in their groups like herds of wildebeests and prides of lions and crashes of rhinos and unkindnesses of ravens and leaps of leopards and wrecks of sea hawks.

quote.citation: 1969 July 20, Neil Armstrong, as he became the first man to step on the moon:
quote.text: That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.

quote.citation: 2024 May 30, Germano Vera Cruz, Elias Aboujaoude, Magdalena Liberacka-Dwojak, Monika Wiłkość-Dębczyńska, Lucien Rochat, Riaz Khan, Yasser Khazaal, “How much online pornography is too much? A comparison of two theoretically distinct assessment scales”, in Archives of Public Health, volume 82, →DOI:
quote.text: Since the arrival of mainstream pornography platforms in the early 2000’s and the rise in smartphone use, online pornography consumption has shown considerable year on year leaps.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A large step in reasoning, often one that is not justified by the facts.
Copulation with, or coverture of, a female beast.

quote.text: Much difference of opinion exists as to the number of bullings a cow should receive. Here, I think, good judgment should be used. If the bull is cool and quiet, and some time has intervened since he had his last cow, one good leap is better than more  […]

definitions.definition: (music) A passing from one note to another by an interval, especially by a long one, or by one including several other intermediate intervals.
A small cataract over which fish attempt to jump; a salmon ladder.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English lep, from Old English lēap (“basket”), from Proto-West Germanic *laup, from Proto-Germanic *laupaz (“container, basket”). Cognate with Icelandic laupur (“basket”).

definitions.definition: A trap or snare for fish, made from twigs; a weely.
